children.text:
Yes. How is it relevant? Like I said I still pay taxes. In fact, quite a bit more than my parents did. It's not me voting for them to not receive an education. It's not my kids disrupting their classes. I'd be happy to vote for a school board full of hard-ass drill instructors that appoint hard-ass drill instructors as superintendents and principals. I'm happy for kids to receive merit scholarships and go study engineering.

This isn't pulling the ladder up behind me. It's noticing a ladder, climbing out of a pit, and walking away. Ladder's still right there. Meanwhile others are asking why we don't try to make ourselves more comfortable in the pit.

> We're gone.

Are you familiar with the phrase "pulling up the ladder behind you"?

My wife and I both come from broken homes. Neither of us came from money. Sure, there are plenty of good people of every class, but if you spend a lot of time around lower class people, you'll learn that a lot of them will very proudly broadcast their poor behavior to everybody. It is precisely because we can empathize a little too well that we know to avoid those kinds of situations as much as possible.

We do our part, and we've decided to live in an area where others also do their part and try to build a community and a society, and not in an area where people tear down the community around them, or make excuses for those who do that. Again, what exactly are you chiding me for? What should I be doing differently? It's not us keeping them down. We're gone.

source.text:
> Not sure what to tell you. It's been a problem for decades and only gets worse

It's been a problem for literally millennia. This hardly unique to 21st century america.

Yes, I'm glad you don't have a "problem child". That's genuinely great, I wish everyone was that lucky.

What I would like, in the smallest possible way, is some shred of empathy for people who aren't as lucky as you are. Perhaps you could practice the concept of "walking a mile in another man's shoes" and make an attempt to understand what they're dealing with instead of dismissing them as inferior.

I'm also happy your wife is volunteering to help with girl scouts. I think that's a great thing and more people should do it.

But that doesn't excuse your lack of empathy.

Kids are not some kind of deterministic automatons where the same input always produces the same output (as if we could even reproduce the same inputs for an entire life). They're more complicated than that for reasons we frankly can't even understand.

There are a number of things that are highly correlated with producing a "good child", a major one being having enough money that the family isn't under constant stress and you can afford second (or third or fourth) chances.

But callously discarding every child who isn't lucky enough to benefit from this is just wrong. We, as a society, a culture, should be better than that.

Am I expecting you, personally, to go out and change the world? No, no more than I'm expecting myself to do it. But we all make small decisions every day and if enough of us make the "right ones" they can add up, and it starts with empathy for our fellow man.
